body:
## Why the Development Calendar Decides Whether an OEM Hijab Program Ships

For an emerging DTC brand, a boutique adding its own label, or a private-label buyer building a hijab range, the distance between a good idea and a container-ready order is not creativity. It is development discipline. Every OEM hijab program moves through the same sequence of gates: tech pack, first sample, sample revisions, approval sign-off, MOQ commitment, capacity booking, bulk production, inspection, and delivery. Sequenced correctly, the program is predictable and financeable. Compressed or run out of order, cost and risk compound quietly until the delivery date becomes impossible and the only remaining lever is expensive air freight.

Most first-time buyers lose time in three predictable places: an incomplete tech pack that forces the factory to guess, an open-ended revision loop with no agreed revision limit, and a capacity booking that was never actually reserved because no deposit was paid. At QiuYan Factory we treat the development calendar as a shared, dated document owned by both the buyer and the factory. This guide walks that calendar gate by gate, with the technical and commercial parameters you can hold any OEM supplier to.

## The OEM Development Calendar, Gate by Gate

Think of the calendar as ten gates. Each gate has an owner, a duration, and an output that must be signed before the next gate opens.

- Gate 0, brief and feasibility (2-4 business days): style, market, target price, quantity band, and delivery window. The factory confirms whether the brief is technically and commercially feasible.
- Gate 1, tech pack locked and quoted (3-5 business days): the buyer issues a complete tech pack, and the factory returns an itemized quotation covering fabric, cut-make-trim, trims, packing, and testing.
- Gate 2, first sample round (5-7 business days): the sampling room builds the first prototype in the specified fabric and color.
- Gate 3, sample revisions (5-7 business days per round, budget two rounds): fit, drape, hand-feel, and measurement corrections are made against the buyer's comments.
- Gate 4, lab dips and color approval (10-14 working days total): dyed swatches are measured instrumentally and a shade band is signed.
- Gate 5, pre-production (PP) sample sign-off (5-7 business days): the reference sample that bulk must match is sealed and retained by both parties.
- Gate 6, MOQ confirmation and capacity booking (deposit-triggered): the purchase order and deposit lock the production slot.
- Gate 7, bulk production (15-20 working days): cutting, sewing, finishing, and pressing.
- Gate 8, final inspection and packing: AQL 2.5 inspection and packing per the approved packing spec.
- Gate 9, dispatch and freight: documentation, booking, and shipment.

Run sequentially without overlap, a program from a clean tech pack to dispatch-ready goods sits in the 10-14 week range, before ocean transit. The mistake is treating these gates as a wish list rather than a schedule. Dated gates, with a named owner on each side, are what convert a calendar into a commitment.

The calendar is not a straight line, and two overlaps are legitimate. Color can run in parallel with construction sampling, because the dyehouse and the sampling room are independent, so a lab dip window and a first-sample window can share the same week. Fabric booking can begin once the tech pack is locked and the fabric is specified, even before the PP sample is signed, provided the buyer accepts the small risk of a specification change. Everything else should stay sequential, because approving a PP sample before the color is settled simply books a re-dye against your own delivery date.

A useful test for any calendar: every gate should end with a document. Gate 1 ends with a signed quotation. Gate 3 ends with comments on a specific round. Gate 4 ends with a signed shade band. Gate 5 ends with a sealed PP sample. Gate 6 ends with a purchase order and deposit receipt. If a gate ends only with a message saying it looks good, it has not really closed.

## The Tech Pack: The Document That Sets Your Price and Your Date

A tech pack is the single document that determines whether a factory can quote accurately and sample quickly. When it is thin, the factory quotes a wide price band to protect itself, and sampling drifts into repeated clarification. A complete OEM hijab tech pack should contain:

- Style and silhouette: shape, length, width, edge finish (rolled hem, overlock, baby hem), and any layering or attachment points.
- Measurement spec: a full point-of-measure chart with a tolerance column. For hijab panels we work to plus or minus 0.5 cm on length and width and plus or minus 0.3 cm on trim placement, unless the buyer specifies tighter.
- Fabric specification: fiber content, exact GSM, construction, and finish. A shade approved on one substrate is not the same color on another, so the substrate must be declared.
- Color references: Pantone FHI TCX chips or physical swatches, plus the required color target and the acceptable color difference.
- Trims and labels: care labels, woven or printed branding, hangtags, and thread color.
- Packaging: polybag, header card, folding, and carton configuration.
- Size grading and assortment: how many colorways and sizes, and the split between them.
- Commercial fields: target quantity, delivery window, Incoterm, and destination.
- Compliance and labeling: the destination market's fiber-content and care-labeling requirements.

If a buyer cannot fill these fields, the honest next step is a paid development round, not a guessing game. A 3-5 business day quoting turnaround is realistic only against a complete pack.

## Fabric, GSM, and Construction: Weaving and Knitting

Hijab fabric falls into two construction families, and the family you choose drives cost, drape, and how the article behaves after washing.

Woven constructions are built on a loom by interlacing warp and weft yarns. The modest-wear staples are chiffon (light, airy, slightly crisp), crepe (matte, fluid, forgiving of creasing), voile (soft and breathable), satin (lustrous and heavier-drape), and twill (structured). Knitted constructions are built by interlocking loops: single jersey, interlock, and rib, which give stretch and recovery that wovens cannot.

Practical GSM bands we run: chiffon 55-75 GSM, voile 60-85 GSM, crepe 90-120 GSM, single jersey 150-190 GSM, interlock 180-220 GSM, and heavy-weight knits above 220 GSM. Always specify a weight tolerance of plus or minus 5% and a usable-width tolerance of plus or minus 2%, because unchecked GSM drift changes drape, opacity, and the finished hand-feel. Also specify shrinkage: no more than 3% in either direction after the agreed wash cycle, tested on the production fabric, not a lab substitute.

For woven articles, state yarn count and density, for example a 50D by 75D warp and weft with a defined picks-per-inch. For knits, state the stitch and the fabric's stretch and recovery at a defined load. These are the numbers that make a fabric order reproducible rather than a lucky match.

## Sample Revisions and Approval Gates

Sampling is not one event; it is a controlled loop with an explicit exit. The first sample proves the concept. The pre-production sample proves that the concept can be manufactured exactly, at the specified construction and color, and becomes the sealed reference for bulk.

Two rules keep the loop from running forever. First, cap the revisions: agree in the purchase order that the price includes two revision rounds, with additional rounds quoted separately at a stated fee. Second, approve against data, not impressions. Each round should be assessed on measurement against the point-of-measure chart, hand-feel and drape against the sealed reference, and color against an instrumental reading.

Color is where most revisions stall. We hold bulk color to Delta E at or below 1.0 as an internal target, at or below 1.5 as the normal commercial acceptance band, and at or below 2.0 only where cross-substrate matching cannot be tightened; any lot above 2.0 is rejected and re-dyed. Specify the equation in the purchase order, Delta E 2000 preferred, and read the DL*, Da*, and Db* components separately so you can see whether a lot is running light, red, or blue rather than merely how far off it is.

At the end of sampling, both parties sign the PP sample. From that moment, bulk quality is measured against a physical reference, and a final AQL 2.5 inspection at the factory confirms that what shipped matches what was approved. AQL 2.5 is the standard commercial sampling plan for major defects: it accepts a defined number of defectives and rejects the lot when the count exceeds the limit, which is exactly the discipline an OEM program needs before goods leave the floor.

## The Handoff Package: What Must Move From Development to Bulk

The factory handoff is the moment development stops being a series of samples and becomes a production order. It fails most often because the buyer believes the file is complete and the factory believes it is not. A clean handoff package removes that argument. It contains the sealed PP sample, the approved shade band, the final measurement chart, the approved fabric and trim cards, the packing specification, and the labeled cartons from the last sample round. It also contains the commercial documents that make the order executable: the signed purchase order, the deposit receipt, the delivery window, and the Incoterm.

Two items are commonly missing. The first is the trim card for labeling, so bulk starts without the care labels that carry the destination market's required fiber and care information, and the line stalls while labels are reprinted. The second is the packing specification, so goods are finished but not packed to the buyer's carton plan and cannot be shipped without repacking. Both are inexpensive to lock at the handoff gate and expensive to fix during bulk.

We recommend a single handoff meeting, or a single handoff document, that lists every approved reference and every outstanding item with a named owner and a due date. When the factory can see, in one place, that the shading is signed, the labels are on order, and the packing spec is final, the 15-20 working day bulk clock starts cleanly instead of stalling on the first day.

## MOQ and Capacity Booking

MOQ is not a single number. It is a ladder tied to fabric sourcing and dyeing, and understanding the ladder lets you plan colorways without surprise surcharges.

- Stock fabric, existing color: from 300 pieces per colorway.
- Stock fabric, custom dye: from 500 pieces per colorway.
- Custom-developed fabric: 1,000-1,500 pieces per colorway, because the mill runs a minimum greige batch.
- Printed programs: 500-1,000 pieces per design, depending on the print method and repeat.

Capacity, not price, is the real constraint in a peak season. A quotation is not a reservation. To actually book a production slot, you need a signed purchase order and a deposit, typically 30% of order value, which triggers fabric booking and line allocation; the balance is due against the shipping documents. During peak windows we recommend booking capacity six to eight weeks ahead of the required bulk start. Once booked, bulk runs 15-20 working days, but that clock only starts when the PP sample and shade band are approved and the fabric is in-house. A program that books capacity before its approvals are closed is buying a suit before it has been measured.

## Delivery Risk Control

Every late hijab order traces back to one of six risks. Each has a control.

- Fabric delay: buy against a dated fabric-in-house milestone, keep a 10-15% buffer, and dual-source critical qualities.
- Dye re-dye: lock the shade band early, and budget the 10-14 working day color window rather than discovering it late.
- Revision loop: cap revisions and approve against measurement and Delta E.
- Capacity bump: reserve the slot with a deposit and confirm the line allocation in writing.
- Inspection failure: run AQL 2.5 before dispatch, not after arrival, so defects are fixed at the source.
- Freight and customs: match the Incoterm to your capability, build in clearance time, and hold an air-freight contingency for the top sellers only.

The single most effective control is a shared, dated gate calendar with the buffer stated openly. A supplier that will show you its line plan and its fabric commitments is a supplier you can plan around. A supplier that will not should be treated as a delivery risk regardless of price.

## Working With QiuYan Factory

QiuYan Factory builds OEM and private-label hijab programs end to end: tech pack review, sampling in 5-7 business days, capped revision rounds, instrumental color approval, standard custom bulk MOQ from 100 pieces per colorway; special constructions may require 300 pieces per colorway, deposit-secured capacity booking, AQL 2.5 inspection, and 15-20 working day bulk. If you are planning a range for the coming season and want a dated development calendar with the gates priced and the risks named, send your brief and target delivery window to melody@wennuanfactory.com or call +86 150 2459 7603. We will return a feasibility read, an itemized quotation, and a calendar you can hold us to.

metaDescription: A factory guide to hijab finishing for wholesale collections: softening, bio-polishing, brushing, calendering, and anti-static, with GSM tolerances, Delta E control, AQL 2.5, 5-7 business day sampling, and 15-20 working day bulk for DTC, boutique, and private-label buyers.

faq.q: Will softening or bio-polishing ruin a hijab's drape?
faq.a: Not if it is applied with limits and measured. Softening and bio-polishing work on the surface and the fiber rather than the structure, so they improve hand-feel with limited drape change when softener add-on is held around 1-3% on weight of fabric and bio-polishing weight loss is capped near 2-5%. The finish that most threatens drape is calendering, because heat and pressure raise bending rigidity. We keep drape coefficient in a 40-65% band and check bending rigidity on a KES-F or FAST system after finishing, always on the production fabric, and hold a sealed hand-feel reference.

faq.q: Which finishing route should I choose for a lightweight summer hijab versus an autumn one?
faq.a: For a lightweight summer hijab and Gulf markets, we usually run a light bio-polish plus a hydrophilic softener, skip calendering to protect the fluid drape, and add a durable anti-static finish. For an autumn or winter article we use a single-pass peach brush on a slightly heavier woven to create a matte, warm hand, then verify drape after brushing because surface friction changes. For a smooth premium crepe we apply a light Schreiner calendering pass calibrated against drape plus a controlled silicone softener. Each route is finished on the line and checked against GSM, drape, and Delta E targets.

faq.q: How long do finishing samples and bulk production take, and how is quality checked?
faq.a: Finishing samples run 5-7 business days per round and are finished on the exact production route so the hand-feel and drape you approve match bulk. Bulk production runs 15-20 working days after the pre-production sample and finishing route are approved. GSM is held to plus or minus 5% and color to Delta E at or below 1.5 for normal acceptance, 1.0 as an internal target. Final inspection uses AQL 2.5 for major and AQL 4.0 for minor defects, with critical defects at zero tolerance. For a quote, contact melody@wennuanfactory.com or +86 150 2459 7603.

body:
## Why Finishing, Not Fiber, Decides How a Hijab Feels

A buyer can spend months choosing between a 95 GSM woven voile and a 110 GSM knit crepe, approve the color, and still open the bulk carton to a hijab that drapes like paper or slips off the head. The reason is almost never the fabric construction. It is the finishing line. Softening, bio-polishing, brushing, calendering, and anti-static treatment are the last operations a hijab passes through before inspection, and they rewrite the two properties a customer judges within three seconds: hand-feel and drape.

For a DTC brand, a boutique, or a private-label buyer building a hijab range for North America, Europe, or the Gulf, finishing is where a technically correct fabric becomes a product that either returns or repeats. It is also where the most expensive mistakes hide, because a finish that makes a swatch feel luxurious on the table can quietly stiffen the cloth, add weight, or kill the fluid fall a hijab depends on. This guide covers the finishing toolkit as we run it at QiuYan Factory: what each finish does mechanically, what it costs in GSM and drape, and how to specify it with tolerances you can actually enforce.

## The Physics You Are Selling: Hand-Feel vs Drape

Hand-feel and drape are different properties driven by different mechanics, and conflating them is the most common specification error we see.

Hand-feel is a surface and compression property. It is governed by fiber fineness, yarn twist, fabric surface friction, and the finish film left on the cloth. It is what the customer feels between the fingers.

Drape is a structural property. It is governed by bending rigidity, shear stiffness, fabric weight, and thickness. It is what makes a hijab fall in soft folds instead of standing away from the head.

A finish can improve one and destroy the other. A heavy silicone softener can make fabric feel wonderful while adding weight that changes how it hangs. A hard calendering pass can deliver a smooth surface while raising bending rigidity enough to remove the fluidity. For that reason we specify every finishing route against measurable targets rather than adjectives:

- Weight: GSM held to plus or minus 5% against the approved standard.
- Drape: drape coefficient percentage, measured on a drape tester, with a typical hijab band of 40-65% depending on the silhouette.
- Bending: bending rigidity in mN.mm on a KES-F or FAST system, used to catch stiffening before bulk runs.
- Air permeability: 80-200 mm/s for breathable lightweight collections.
- Surface: friction and roughness indices, or an agreed physical handle reference kept sealed beside the sample.

The rule we give every buyer is simple: approve a finish on the production fabric, never on a swatch of a different construction, and never from a photograph.

## Softening Systems: Silicone, Cationic, and Hydrophilic

Softening is the most requested finish and the easiest to over-apply. Softeners deposit a lubricating film on the fiber surface that lowers friction between yarns, letting them slide instead of lock. That sliding is what the hand reads as softness.

Three families cover most hijab programs:

- Non-ionic and cationic softeners give a full, cushioned hand and work well on woven voile and challis. They are efficient but can yellow under heat and are not ideal for whites.
- Silicone softeners, amino-functional and block types, deliver a slick, silky hand and improve crease recovery. Amino silicones give the strongest softness but can shift shade on pale and pastel colors, so every treated lot must be re-read against the Delta E band.
- Hydrophilic softeners preserve moisture management and wicking, which matters for humid Gulf markets and for athletic-adjacent modest wear.

The drape trap in softening is weight gain. A softener add-on of 1-3% on weight of fabric is normal; above that, the fabric gains body and the drape coefficient climbs. We cap softener add-on and re-measure drape after finishing, not before, because the two numbers rarely move together.

## Bio-Polishing: Enzyme Smoothing Without Surprises

Bio-polishing uses cellulase enzymes to nibble away protruding fiber ends on cellulosic fabrics such as cotton, viscose, and their blends, producing a permanently smooth surface and a softer hand that survives repeated laundering. Unlike a softener film, bio-polishing changes the fiber itself, so the effect does not wash out.

Two parameters decide whether bio-polishing helps or hurts a hijab:

- Weight loss. A controlled bio-polish removes roughly 2-5% of fabric weight. On a 90 GSM voile that is up to 4.5 GSM, a real change in hand and a small transparency risk, so we test air permeability and opacity after treatment and keep the finished GSM inside the plus or minus 5% band.
- Strength loss. Enzymatic action can reduce tear and tensile strength. We require treated fabric to retain at least 80% of untreated tear strength, verified per batch.

Bio-polishing pairs well with a light silicone softener on woven voile, giving a smooth, cool hand without a heavy film. It is a poor choice for very low GSM sheers where transparency is already a concern.

## Brushing and Peach Finish: Surface Hand Without Losing Body

Brushing raises fine fiber ends to create a sueded, peach-skin surface. On hijab it delivers a matte, velvet-touch effect that photographs beautifully and feels warm, which suits autumn and winter collections.

Brushing is a mechanical finish, so its effect is set by roller speed, contact pressure, and the number of passes. Over-brushing is the main risk: it can thin the fabric, reduce GSM, and encourage pilling. We set a light single-pass peach finish for hijabs, verify GSM before and after, and hold the final weight inside the plus or minus 5% band.

Because brushing alters surface friction, it changes hand-feel far more than drape. That makes it a useful tool when you want a differentiated touch while protecting the fall of the cloth, but it must be tested for pilling and for how it interacts with folding, packaging, and any inner layer worn beneath it.

## Calendering and Schreiner: Gloss, Density, and the Drape Trap

Calendering passes fabric between heated rollers under pressure to flatten the surface, close the weave, and add luster. A Schreiner calender, with its engraved roller, produces a subtle pearlescent sheen and a closed, smoother hand; a flat calender produces a general gloss.

Calendering is where drape is most often damaged. Pressure and heat increase fiber packing and bonding, which raises bending rigidity and makes the cloth stiffer and papery. The tighter you calender for shine, the more the fabric stands away from the head instead of falling.

Our approach is to calibrate calendering against drape, not just gloss. We run a series of pressure settings, measure drape coefficient and bending rigidity at each, and pick the lightest pass that still delivers the target surface. For sheer, fluid silhouettes we often skip calendering entirely and achieve surface character through bio-polishing or a light softener instead.

## Anti-Static Finishing: Comfort in Dry, Heated Markets

Synthetic hijab fabrics such as polyester crepe, jersey, and chiffon build static in dry, air-conditioned interiors and heated winter rooms, the exact environments of many European and North American customers. Static makes a hijab cling, crackle, and slip, which reads as cheap regardless of how good the base fabric is.

Anti-static is delivered two ways: a durable hydrophilic finish that raises surface conductivity so charge dissipates, or a temporary antistat that helps in cutting and sewing but fades after a few washes. For a product finish, specify the durable route and confirm the surface resistivity target with the supplier before bulk.

Anti-static finishes are hygroscopic and generally drape-neutral, which makes them one of the safest additions to a lightweight program. The one caution is compatibility with silicone softeners, which can mask the effect. When both are required, apply the anti-static first or specify a combined system and verify static decay on the finished cloth.

## Drape Control: Compaction, Sanforizing, and the Tolerance Stack

If softening, brushing, and calendering are the finishes customers feel, compaction and sanforizing are the finishes that keep the product honest. These mechanical processes control residual shrinkage and stabilize the cloth, so the hijab a customer receives after a few washes keeps the dimensions and drape you approved.

Sanforizing pre-shrinks woven fabric so residual shrinkage stays within about 3% warp and weft. Compaction does similar work for knits. Both are drape-relevant because they change density and can add slight body, so we spec them as part of the finishing route and measure drape after, never before.

The practical danger is the tolerance stack. Weight tolerance, shrinkage tolerance, and color tolerance interact. A 5% weight gain from softener, 3% shrinkage, and a shade step near the Delta E limit can compound into a hijab that looks and feels different from the approved sample even though each individual number technically passed. That is why we audit the finished article as a whole and hold a sealed, signed reference for both hand-feel and drape.

## Specifying Finishing So the Factory Cannot Guess

Finishing is only enforceable if it is written down. A finishing section in the tech pack should carry:

- Fiber and construction: woven plain weave, twill, or knit, with yarn count and fabric GSM plus tolerance.
- Finish route in sequence: for example, bio-polish, then softener at a stated add-on, then compaction, then anti-static.
- Hand-feel and drape standards: a physical sealed reference plus measured drape coefficient and bending rigidity bands.
- Color: fabric target and acceptable Delta E, with the equation named, held to at or below 1.5 for normal acceptance and 1.0 as an internal target.
- Performance: residual shrinkage limits, air permeability, and strength retention after bio-polishing.
- Destination compliance: labeling and any restricted-substance limits for the destination market.

## How We Control the Line: Sampling, Bulk, and Inspection

Finishing is verified at two moments: the sample stage and the bulk stage.

Sampling runs 5-7 business days per round. We finish the sample through the exact production route, same softener, same bio-polish recipe, same calendering pressure, because a sample finished differently tells you nothing about bulk. Most finishing disputes we see trace back to a sample that was hand-finished in the lab rather than run on the line.

Bulk production runs 15-20 working days after the pre-production sample and finishing route are approved. During bulk we verify GSM, drape coefficient, and shade at defined intervals, and hold finished rolls against the sealed reference.

Final inspection uses AQL 2.5 for major defects and AQL 4.0 for minor defects on finished goods, with critical defects at zero tolerance. Inspectors check for shading through the roll, brushing streaks, calendering marks, static cling on folded panels, and hand-feel consistency, not just stitching and measurements. Any lot outside the agreed GSM or Delta E band is held before packing.

## A Practical Decision Path

When a buyer asks which finishes to use, we work backward from the silhouette and the market:

- A fluid, lightweight drape for summer and the Gulf: a light bio-polish plus a hydrophilic softener, no calendering, plus durable anti-static.
- A smooth, premium everyday crepe: a light calendering pass calibrated to drape, plus a controlled silicone softener and anti-static.
- A matte, tactile autumn article: a single-pass peach brush on a slightly heavier woven, plus a softener, with drape verified after brushing.

No route is universal. The correct answer is always the one that hits your drape target and your hand-feel reference at the lowest defensible weight and stiffness, verified on the production fabric.

## Working With QiuYan Factory

QiuYan Factory builds hijab fabric and finished hijabs for DTC brands, boutiques, and private-label and OEM buyers across North America, Europe, and the Gulf. We finish on the production line, not in a lab, and we approve hand-feel and drape against a sealed reference before bulk. For finishing specifications, sample requests, or a development quote, contact melody@wennuanfactory.com or reach us on WhatsApp at +86 150 2459 7603.

title: Hijab Size Grading and Finished Dimensions: A Factory Specification Guide for Wholesale and OEM Buyers
metaTitle: Hijab Size Grading and Dimensions Guide for Wholesale OEM Buyers
metaDescription: A factory-side guide to hijab size grading: define finished dimensions, fabric width, tolerance, shrinkage allowance, market-specific proportions, GSM and QC checks before bulk production.
heroAlt: hijab size grading and finished dimensions wholesale factory specification guide

faq.q: What is the standard wholesale hijab size for a first production order?
faq.a: A common starting specification is 180 × 70 cm, but the correct size depends on the fabric, edge finish, target market and styling brief. Confirm the finished size after washing rather than approving only the cutting size. QiuYan Factory can develop custom dimensions, including smaller children's proportions, with a one-piece approval sample before the standard 100-piece-per-colour bulk MOQ.

faq.q: How much size tolerance should a buyer specify for modal and jersey hijabs?
faq.a: A practical starting point is ±2 cm on length and width for standard modal or jersey programs, subject to the approved sample and wash-test result. Buyers should write the tolerance, measurement method and post-wash condition into the purchase specification so the factory and inspection team measure the same way.

faq.q: Can a factory grade one hijab pattern into several market sizes?
faq.a: Yes. A factory can create a controlled size set by changing length, width, corner geometry and finishing allowance while keeping the same design language. Each size should have its own approved measurement sheet, marker plan, sample and packaging label to prevent mixed-SKU production.

body:
## Why Finished Dimensions Decide Whether a Hijab Sells

A hijab can use the correct fibre, print and colour and still underperform if its finished dimensions are wrong. A scarf that is too short may not give a customer enough wrapping coverage. A scarf that is too wide may feel bulky around the neck or consume more packaging volume than the brand planned. A sample can look perfect on a model and still fail when the buyer measures the bulk shipment after washing.

For wholesale and private-label buyers, size is therefore not a decorative detail. It is a production specification that affects fabric yield, sewing allowances, shipping cartons, product photography, customer expectations and return rates. The most reliable approach is to approve dimensions as a controlled system: define the finished measurement, record the tolerance, account for shrinkage, and verify the result at several points in production.

This factory-side guide explains how QiuYan Factory approaches hijab size grading for modal, jersey, chiffon and embellished programs. It covers the difference between fabric width and finished scarf width, how to write a measurement sheet, how GSM and edge construction affect proportion, how to build market-specific size options, and how to connect approval samples with AQL 2.5 shipment inspection.

## 1. Separate Fabric Width from Finished Product Size

The first common mistake in a buyer brief is treating the fabric width as the final scarf width. A mill may supply fabric in an open width, while the finished hijab loses material through cutting, edge alignment, hemming or trim placement. A 70 cm finished scarf may require a wider cutting plan depending on the edge construction and the fabric’s usable width.

A technical specification should record at least four different measurements:

1. **Usable fabric width:** the width available after removing the selvedge or unstable edge.
2. **Cutting size:** the rectangle or shaped piece cut before finishing.
3. **Finished size:** the measurement after hemming, trimming, pressing and final inspection.
4. **Post-wash size:** the measurement after the agreed care-test condition.

For a standard lightweight modal program, a buyer may request a finished size of 180 × 70 cm. That number is not enough on its own. The buyer should also state whether the length is measured from finished corner to corner, whether the width is measured at the centre or along the short edge, and whether the measurement is taken before or after washing.

For a rectangular product, we normally measure the scarf flat on a clean table without stretching it. For a triangular or specially shaped product, the measurement sheet should show a simple diagram with named points. This prevents a factory operator, buyer and third-party inspector from interpreting “length” differently.

## 2. Build a Size Grading System Instead of Random Size Changes

Size grading means creating a controlled family of dimensions from one approved base specification. It is different from making one scarf longer because a buyer sends a message asking for “a little more coverage.” Random changes create inconsistent cutting markers and make it difficult to compare samples with bulk.

A controlled grading table might include:

| Size code | Finished length | Finished width | Intended use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| S | 160 cm | 60 cm | compact styling or younger customer profile |
| M | 180 cm | 70 cm | core wholesale size |
| L | 195 cm | 75 cm | fuller wrap and premium styling |

The values above are development examples, not a universal market standard. The buyer should select the range from customer feedback, model testing and the intended styling. The important point is that each size must have a separate code, measurement tolerance and approval sample.

For a DTC brand, a three-size range can create a clearer product page than a vague “one size fits all” claim. For a boutique buyer, however, one core size may be more efficient if the store wants a simple stock-keeping unit system. The factory can support either approach, but the production documents must state which approach has been approved.

## 3. How GSM Changes Perceived Size and Drape

GSM means grams per square metre, or the mass of the fabric over a standard area. It does not directly define the scarf’s finished dimensions, but it changes how those dimensions behave in use.

A 60–80 GSM modal scarf can appear more generous because it collapses into soft folds and drapes around the shoulder. A 130–160 GSM stretch jersey scarf has more body and recovery, so the same 180 × 70 cm rectangle may feel more compact when wrapped. A 55–75 GSM chiffon scarf may need additional width or a carefully selected edge finish because its light body and slip can change how much usable coverage the wearer perceives.

This is why a buyer should not copy the same size from modal to jersey without a wear trial. The physical measurement may match, while the wrapping behaviour does not. In a sample review, check forehead coverage, chin coverage, shoulder drop, pin placement and the amount of fabric remaining after one complete wrap. Record those observations next to the numerical measurements.

## 4. Allow for Shrinkage Before You Approve the Marker

Shrinkage allowance must be calculated before bulk cutting, not after the shipment arrives. Modal, cotton and regenerated cellulosic fibres can respond differently to moisture, heat and drying. Jersey can also change through relaxation of stretch and knit structure.

For each fabric, the development sample should be measured before and after the agreed wash test. Record length change and width change separately. A scarf that loses 2% in length but only 0.5% in width will need a different cutting allowance from a scarf that changes evenly in both directions. The buyer should not accept a supplier’s generic “low shrinkage” statement as a substitute for a measurement report.

A practical approval record includes:

- Fabric composition and construction.
- Target GSM and tolerance.
- Cutting dimensions.
- Finished dimensions before washing.
- Finished dimensions after the agreed wash cycle.
- Drying and ironing condition.
- Acceptance tolerance for the approved size.

For example, if the approved post-wash size is 180 × 70 cm, the cutting plan may need to be larger to compensate for expected relaxation. The actual allowance depends on the fabric and finishing process. It should be calculated from the factory’s test result, not inserted as an unverified fixed percentage.

## 5. Edge Finishing Changes the Final Measurement

The edge is where size control becomes practical. A baby rolled hem, pin hem, overlock, hand-rolled silk edge, lace trim or tassel treatment uses a different amount of material and applies a different tension to the scarf.

On a lightweight modal scarf, an unstable edge can curl inward and make the product measure smaller than the cutting pattern. On a lace-edge design, the trim can add weight along the long sides and pull the base fabric into a slight wave. On a tassel design, fringe length should be recorded separately from the fabric body so the buyer knows whether the advertised length includes the finished fringe.

For each edge type, the specification should include:

1. Edge construction name.
2. Target visible width or trim width.
3. Seam allowance or fold allowance.
4. Corner treatment.
5. Measurement point after pressing.
6. Visual acceptance standard for waviness, puckering and loose threads.

A size sheet that says only “neat hem” is not production-ready. The operator needs a measurable construction, and the inspector needs a visible standard.

## 6. Market-Specific Proportions Need Wear Testing

Buyers serving the Gulf, Europe, North America or Southeast Asia may receive different customer feedback on the same scarf size. Climate, layering, styling habits, garment silhouettes and customer height all influence the preferred proportion. However, a factory should not turn a market stereotype into an unsupported fixed claim. The safe process is to test a small size set with the buyer’s actual customers or model references.

A buyer can compare three prototypes using the same fabric, print and edge finish:

- A compact option for lighter coverage and lower packaging volume.
- A core option for everyday styling.
- A fuller option for layered wrapping and longer drape.

Photograph each prototype in the same camera setup and record the exact measurements. This lets the brand review the difference without confusing size changes with colour, print scale or fabric weight. If the artwork is directional, verify that the print repeat remains visually balanced on every graded size.

## 7. Print Scale and Pattern Placement Across Sizes

A print designed for a 180 × 70 cm scarf can look crowded or too empty when transferred to a different proportion. A large floral motif may be cropped at the border of a longer scarf. A small geometric repeat may become visually noisy on a compact size.

Before approving size grading, ask the factory to confirm whether the artwork will be:

- Scaled proportionally.
- Kept at the same motif size with more or fewer repeats.
- Repositioned around a border or corner.
- Adapted for a directional layout.

The print file should have a named revision. The size sheet should reference that revision so a production operator does not use the artwork for the original size on a new marker. For reactive or digital printing, colour approval should still be checked against the approved standard, with a practical Delta E target agreed by the buyer and factory. A target such as ΔE ≤ 2.0 may be appropriate for a controlled colour program, but the actual acceptance limit belongs in the signed approval record.

## 8. Turning the Specification into a Tech Pack

A tech pack is the controlled document that translates the buyer’s product idea into production instructions. For a hijab, the dimension page should include a flat sketch, measurement points, tolerances, fabric details, edge construction and packaging fold direction.

At minimum, include:

- Style name and SKU code.
- Fabric composition and target GSM.
- Finished length and width for every size.
- Measurement tolerance in centimetres.
- Pre-wash and post-wash condition.
- Edge finish and visible trim dimensions.
- Print or colour artwork revision.
- Label placement and fold direction.
- Sample approval date and revision number.

The factory should return a marked measurement sheet with the pre-production sample. If the buyer changes the length after approval, issue a new revision rather than editing an old file informally. This protects both parties when several colourways or sizes are produced at the same time.

## 9. Quality Control: Measuring Bulk Without Creating False Rejections

AQL 2.5 is a sampling system used to assess whether a production lot meets the agreed quality level. It does not replace a clear size specification. If the tolerance is not written, an inspector cannot determine whether a two-centimetre difference is acceptable or a defect.

For bulk inspection, define:

1. How many pieces are measured from the selected sample.
2. Which measurement points are checked.
3. Whether the scarf is relaxed, pressed or washed before measurement.
4. What tolerance applies to length, width and trim placement.
5. How size labels are matched to the physical dimensions.

A factory can use in-line checks during cutting and sewing, followed by final measurement checks before packing. The objective is to identify drift early, when correction is possible, rather than discover a mixed size run during container loading.

Alongside dimensions, inspect GSM against the approved range, colour against the approved standard, edge tension, print placement, loose threads and packaging labels. A product can pass its length measurement and still create a return problem if the label identifies the wrong size or the print is positioned inconsistently.

## 10. Sample and Bulk Timing for a Size-Graded Program

A one-piece approval sample is useful for confirming the base fabric, proportions and edge finish. If the order contains three sizes, however, the buyer should request or approve a size set rather than assume that one approved size automatically proves the others.

A practical development sequence is:

- Initial specification review: one to two working days.
- First sample: approximately 5–7 working days, depending on fabric and trim availability.
- Size-set revision: another 5–7 working days when a new marker or edge adjustment is required.
- Bulk production: commonly 15–35 working days after final approval, depending on style complexity, fabric availability and order volume.
- Final inspection and packing: scheduled before the agreed shipping date.

These are planning references, not a guarantee for every SKU. A special lace, tassel, custom print or unusual size can change the timeline. Confirm the actual schedule in the quotation and purchase order.

## 11. Buyer Checklist Before Placing the Bulk Order

Before releasing a production order, confirm that the supplier has written down:

- Finished dimensions, not only cutting dimensions.
- A tolerance for every measurement.
- Pre-wash and post-wash conditions.
- Fabric composition, GSM and usable width.
- Edge construction and visible trim size.
- Print scale, placement and artwork revision.
- Size codes, labels and carton packing ratio.
- One-piece approval sample or approved size set.
- Standard custom bulk MOQ of 100 pieces per colour, with any 300-piece special-construction requirement stated in the quotation.
- AQL 2.5 inspection method and final measurement points.

This checklist turns “please make it slightly bigger” into an executable factory brief. It also gives the buyer evidence to compare the sample, bulk production and final shipment.

## Factory Support for Size-Graded Private Label Programs

QiuYan Factory develops modal, jersey, chiffon and embellished hijab programs for wholesale, private-label and OEM/ODM buyers. Our team can review your finished size, fabric composition, GSM target, edge construction, print artwork and packaging requirement before sampling.

For standard custom bulk, the usual MOQ is 100 pieces per colour. A one-piece approval sample can be made first, and special constructions may require 300 pieces per colour after the specification is confirmed. Sampling is typically 5–7 working days, while bulk timing depends on the confirmed style and order volume.

Send your size sheet, reference sample or target measurements to **melody@wennuanfactory.com**. You can also message QiuYan Factory on **WhatsApp +86 150 2459 7603** with the product category, target dimensions, fabric preference and estimated quantity. We will return a practical sampling plan, measurement confirmation and lead-time estimate before bulk production begins.

title: Instant and Slip-On Hijabs: A Factory Guide to Ready-to-Wear Construction, Sizing, and Wholesale OEM Sourcing
metaTitle: Instant & Slip-On Hijab Manufacturing Guide for Wholesale Buyers
metaDescription: A factory-side guide to instant and slip-on hijabs: ready-to-wear construction, sewn-in caps, jersey GSM, stitch standards, sizing, AQL 2.5 QC, MOQ and lead times for wholesale and OEM buyers.
heroAlt: Folded ready-to-wear instant and slip-on hijabs on a factory inspection table for wholesale OEM sourcing

faq.q: What is the difference between an instant hijab and a slip-on hijab in manufacturing terms?
faq.a: Both are ready-to-wear, but the construction differs. An instant hijab is a pre-sewn piece — usually a jersey tube or a shaped scarf with a stitched-in cap area — that the wearer pulls on without pins. A slip-on hijab (sometimes called a pull-on or al-amira two-piece) typically pairs a fitted tube cap with a separate draped layer. From a factory view, the instant style is one integrated sewing operation with a bonded or sewn-in forehead edge, while the slip-on is two coordinated pieces that must match in GSM, color (within ΔE 1.0 cross-piece), and shrinkage. We confirm which construction you want in the tech pack before sampling. Questions: melody@wennuanfactory.com or WhatsApp +86 150 2459 7603.

faq.q: What fabric weight and stitch standards do you use for instant hijabs?
faq.a: For jersey instant hijabs we most often use 180-220 GSM cotton or viscose jersey with 4-6% elastane for recovery, giving a soft but structured pull-on fit. Modal pull-on styles run lighter at 150-180 GSM. Seams use flatlock or coverstitch at 12-14 stitches per inch (SPI) so the forehead and neck edges stay flat against the skin with no scratchy overlock ridge. Elastic recovery is tested so the cap does not bag out after wear. Finished dimensional tolerance is +/- 1 cm on cap circumference and +/- 2 cm on drape length.

faq.q: What are the MOQ, sampling, and bulk lead times for instant hijabs?
faq.a: A one-piece approval sample is available in 5-7 working days. Standard custom bulk MOQ is 100 pcs per color; special constructions (bonded edges, custom sewn-in caps, or two-piece slip-on sets) may require 300 pcs per color, confirmed in the quotation. Bulk production runs 25-35 working days depending on fabric dyeing and order size. We inspect to AQL 2.5 before shipment. To start, email melody@wennuanfactory.com or message WhatsApp +86 150 2459 7603.

body:
Instant and slip-on hijabs have moved from a convenience sub-category to a core line for many DTC modest-fashion brands. Younger buyers, new reverts, athletes, and busy professionals increasingly want a ready-to-wear piece they can pull on in seconds without pins, under-caps, or styling. For a brand, that demand is an opportunity — but only if the product is built correctly. A badly constructed instant hijab bags at the cap, scratches at the forehead seam, or twists out of shape after three washes, and the returns follow quickly.

This guide explains how an instant or slip-on hijab is actually made at the factory level: construction types, fabric and weight choices, stitch and edge standards, sizing logic, quality control, and the commercial terms (MOQ, sampling, lead time) a wholesale or OEM buyer should plan around. The goal is to help you write a tech pack that produces a product your customers keep.

## Part 1: What 'instant' and 'slip-on' actually mean

The terms are used loosely in the market, so the first job is to pin down the construction, because each one costs and behaves differently.

**Instant hijab (one-piece).** A pre-sewn scarf — often a jersey tube or a shaped rectangle — with a stitched-in or bonded forehead edge so it frames the face without an under-cap. The wearer pulls it over the head and the drape falls into place. This is one integrated sewing operation.

**Slip-on / pull-on (two-piece, al-amira style).** A fitted tube cap plus a separate draped hood or scarf layer. The two pieces must be color-matched within ΔE 1.0, use the same or compatible GSM, and shrink at the same rate so they still look like a set after washing.

**Jersey wrap-style instant.** A long jersey piece with a sewn band that gives wrap-and-tuck styling without pins. Slightly more fabric, one seam operation.

Before we sample anything, we confirm which of these you mean in the tech pack. A brand that writes only 'instant hijab' and leaves the rest to the factory usually gets back a sample that is close but not what they imagined. Specifying the construction removes a full sampling cycle.

## Part 2: Fabric and weight selection

Ready-to-wear hijabs live or die on fabric choice, because the fabric does the work that pins used to do — it has to hold shape and sit against the skin all day.

**Cotton / viscose jersey (180-220 GSM, 4-6% elastane).** The workhorse for instant and slip-on styles. The elastane gives the recovery that keeps the cap snug; the GSM gives enough body that the drape does not cling. Below ~170 GSM the piece feels flimsy and shows head shape; above ~230 GSM it gets warm and bulky at the cap.

**Modal jersey (150-180 GSM).** A lighter, more fluid pull-on for warmer climates and a dressier drape. Softer hand, more sheen, slightly less structure — we usually add a touch more elastane to compensate for recovery.

**Bamboo viscose blends.** Chosen for breathability and a cool hand, popular for sport-adjacent and summer lines. Needs careful shrinkage control (bamboo viscose can move 5-7% if not pre-shrunk), so we pre-wash the knit before cutting.

For any of these, elastane recovery is a measured property, not a guess. We test that the cap returns to within 2% of its relaxed circumference after stretch cycling, because that number is what stops the hijab bagging out at the hairline after a month of wear.

## Part 3: Construction and stitch standards

The difference between a cheap instant hijab and a premium one is almost entirely in the seams and edges, because those are the parts that touch the skin and take the stress of pulling on.

**Forehead / face edge.** This is the critical edge. We use a flatlock or coverstitch finish, or a bonded (ultrasonic/heat-sealed) edge for a seamless premium look, so there is no raised overlock ridge scratching the forehead. A standard 3-thread overlock here is the single most common complaint driver on budget instant hijabs.

**Seam stitch density.** 12-14 stitches per inch (SPI) on structural seams. Too few and the seam grins open under pull-on stress; too many and the knit puckers.

**Cap seam.** For slip-on two-piece styles the tube cap seam is flatlock so it lies flat against the skull with no pressure line. We also check that the cap seam is positioned to sit above the ear, not on it.

**Hem and drape edges.** Baby-rolled, coverstitched, or raw-cut-and-bonded depending on the look. Jersey can be left clean-cut if the knit is stable, which many minimalist brands prefer.

**Thread and elastane behavior.** We match thread stretch to the fabric so seams flex with the knit instead of snapping or creating a rigid line.

Every one of these is written into the tech pack with a named stitch type and SPI so the sample and the bulk match. If your current supplier cannot tell you the SPI and edge type they use, that is a sign the product is being made to a price, not a standard.

## Part 4: Sizing and grading

Instant and slip-on hijabs are closer to apparel than to flat scarves, because the cap has to fit a head, so sizing matters more than it does for a plain square.

**Cap circumference.** The fitted cap is typically graded across S/M/L (roughly 54 / 56 / 58 cm relaxed), or offered as a single stretch-to-fit size when the elastane content is high enough to cover the range. We confirm which model you want — single size is simpler to stock, graded sizes fit better and reduce returns for a premium line.

**Drape length.** Instant hijabs are usually offered in shorter (around 70-75 cm fall) and longer (85-95 cm fall) options. We set finished-length tolerance at +/- 2 cm.

**Market fit.** Gulf buyers often prefer a longer, fuller drape; European and North American DTC lines frequently want a shorter, sportier fall. We can grade the same cap to different drape lengths per market without re-tooling the cap pattern.

Grading is captured in the tech pack as a size chart with tolerances, so bulk production holds the fit you approved in sampling rather than drifting.

## Part 5: Quality control

Because a ready-to-wear hijab is a fitted, worn product, QC covers both the fabric and the construction, and we inspect to AQL 2.5 before shipment.

**Dimensional checks.** Cap circumference +/- 1 cm, drape length +/- 2 cm, measured on a sampled percentage of the batch.

**Seam and edge checks.** Flatlock/coverstitch integrity, no skipped stitches, no raised forehead ridge, seam strength under pull-on stress.

**Recovery and pilling.** Elastane recovery to within 2% of relaxed cap size; pilling tested on the jersey face so the cap does not fuzz where it rubs the hairline.

**Colorfastness and shrinkage.** Wash-tested so a two-piece slip-on set still matches (within ΔE 1.0 cross-piece) and still fits after laundering; shrinkage held within the pre-approved allowance.

**Color consistency.** ΔE 1.0 against the approved lab dip, and crucially cross-piece for slip-on sets so the cap and drape do not drift apart in tone.

The inspection standard and the specific checks are agreed before bulk, so 'passed QC' means the same thing to you and to us.

## Part 6: Working with the factory — MOQ, sampling, lead time

Here is what a wholesale or OEM program looks like in practice.

**Sampling.** A one-piece approval sample is available in 5-7 working days once the tech pack and fabric are confirmed. For a new construction (bonded edge, custom sewn-in cap, two-piece set) we may do one revision round before you approve bulk.

**MOQ.** Standard custom bulk MOQ is 100 pcs per color. Special constructions — bonded forehead edges, custom sewn-in caps, or coordinated two-piece slip-on sets — may require 300 pcs per color, confirmed in the quotation. The minimum applies per colorway, so you can plan several colors within one purchase order.

**Bulk lead time.** 25-35 working days depending on whether the fabric is stock or dyed-to-order and the size of the run.

**Private label.** We handle sewn-in brand labels, care labels with fiber content and wash symbols, and retail-ready packaging per your spec, so the product arrives ready to sell under your brand.

**What to send us.** The construction type (instant one-piece / slip-on two-piece / wrap), target fabric and GSM, cap sizing model (single stretch size or graded S/M/L), drape length, edge finish, colors with references, and your label and packaging requirements. The more of this is defined up front, the fewer sampling rounds you pay for.

## Part 7: Common failure points and how we design them out

Most instant-hijab returns trace back to a short list of avoidable defects, and knowing them helps you brief the factory precisely.

**Cap bagging.** Caused by too little elastane or poor recovery testing. We fix it by specifying 4-6% elastane and stretch-cycling the cap before approval. If a sample bags in testing, it will bag worse at scale.

**Scratchy forehead edge.** Caused by a raw overlock seam at the face. We fix it with flatlock, coverstitch, or a bonded edge. This single detail drives a disproportionate share of one-star reviews on budget instant hijabs.

**Twisting after wash.** Caused by unbalanced knit tension or uncontrolled shrinkage. We fix it by pre-shrinking the knit and matching panel grain direction, and we wash-test before bulk.

**Cross-piece color drift on slip-on sets.** The cap and drape are often cut from different fabric lots. We fix it by dyeing both pieces from the same lot and checking ΔE 1.0 cross-piece, not just against the standard.

**Cap seam pressing on the ear.** A positioning error. We fix it by setting the seam above the ear line in the pattern, confirmed on the fit sample.

Designing these out at the tech-pack stage is far cheaper than discovering them through returns.

## Part 8: Returns, conversion, and packaging

For a DTC brand, an instant hijab is a trust product: it is often a customer's first pin-free purchase, and the experience decides whether they reorder. A cap that fits, an edge that does not scratch, and a drape that holds shape after washing are what convert a trial buyer into a repeat buyer. That is why the construction standards above are commercial decisions, not just technical ones.

Packaging reinforces the same trust. We offer retail-ready folding, branded sleeves or boxes, and care labels that clearly show fiber content and wash symbols, so the unboxing matches the brand's price positioning. For subscription and gift-set programs, we can coordinate multi-piece packs with consistent sizing and color so the set reads as curated rather than assorted. Clear care guidance printed on the label also reduces wash-related returns, because many instant-hijab complaints are really laundering mistakes, not product defects.

## Conclusion

Instant and slip-on hijabs reward brands that treat them as ready-to-wear apparel rather than as scarves. The fabric weight, the elastane recovery, the forehead edge finish, the stitch density, and the cap sizing are what separate a product customers reorder from one that gets returned. Specify those in the tech pack, confirm them in a sample, and hold them with AQL 2.5 QC, and you have a line that scales.

QiuYan Factory produces instant, slip-on, and wrap-style hijabs in modal, jersey, bamboo viscose, and Tencel Lyocell for DTC brands, boutiques, and OEM/ODM buyers across Europe, the Gulf, and North America. To request a sample or discuss a program, email melody@wennuanfactory.com or message WhatsApp +86 150 2459 7603.

body:
The economics of launching a modest-fashion brand have shifted. In 2026, DTC brands are moving away from broad seasonal assortments and toward leaner, data-led inventory — testing styles in small quantities, reading real sell-through, and reordering only the winners. The logic is simple: inventory ties up cash, and a hijab that sits in a warehouse is a worse outcome than one you never over-ordered. For a brand owner on Instagram or TikTok, the ability to launch a style small, see if it moves, and scale fast is now a competitive advantage.

That strategy only works if the factory behind it supports it. A supplier geared only for large, slow bulk runs forces brands into exactly the over-commitment they are trying to avoid. This guide explains how low-MOQ, small-batch, and quick-response (QR) manufacturing actually works at the factory level — the order sizes, the sampling and reorder lead times, the real cost trade-offs, and how to structure a test-and-scale program without sacrificing quality.

## Part 1: Why small-batch sourcing wins in 2026

The shift is driven by three pressures that every DTC modest-fashion brand feels at once.

**Cash and inventory risk.** Every unit you produce is cash converted into stock. If it does not sell, that cash is frozen — or discounted away. Small batches keep more cash liquid and let a brand spread it across more styles, more tests, more chances to find a winner.

**Trend speed.** Social-driven demand moves in weeks, not seasons. A print or color can spike from a single viral post. Brands that committed to huge bulk runs six months ahead cannot react; brands that test small and reorder fast can ride the wave.

**SKU proliferation.** Modern modest-fashion ranges carry more colors, finishes, and styles than ever. Testing each one in a small batch is the only sane way to learn which SKUs deserve inventory, rather than guessing and over-producing across the board.

The factory's job is to make that test-and-scale loop cheap and fast. That means a workable MOQ, quick samples, and — critically — fast reorders on proven styles.

## Part 2: What 'low MOQ' really means at a hijab factory

MOQ (minimum order quantity, the smallest number of pieces a factory will produce in one run) is the number most brands fixate on, but the nuance matters.

**Standard custom MOQ: 100 pcs per color.** For most jersey and modal styles, 100 pieces per colorway is both our standard bulk minimum and a sensible test quantity. It is enough to populate a product page, fulfil early orders, and read genuine sell-through — without the cash exposure of a 1,000-piece commitment.

**Special constructions: 300 pcs per color.** Styles with higher setup cost — bonded edges, two-piece slip-on sets, custom jacquard weaves — carry a higher minimum because the tooling and machine-setup time has to be amortized over the run. We flag this in the quotation so there are no surprises.

**Per-color logic.** The MOQ applies per colorway, not per order. A brand testing 5 colors orders 5 x 100 = 500 pcs. This is deliberate: dyeing is batched by color, and each shade is a separate dye lot held to ΔE 1.0.

**The honest trade-off.** A smaller run costs more per piece than a large one, because fixed costs (setup, dyeing minimums, inspection) spread over fewer units. We are transparent about this. The small-batch premium is the price of lower inventory risk — and for a brand testing demand, that is usually a good trade. Once a style proves itself, scaling up brings the per-unit cost down.

## Part 3: The test-and-scale workflow

Here is how a quick-response program runs in practice, step by step.

**Step 1 — Sample (5-7 working days).** Once the tech pack and fabric are confirmed, we produce an approval sample in 5-7 working days. You check hand, drape, color, and finish against your brief before committing to any batch.

**Step 2 — Test batch (100 pcs per color).** You order a small batch of the approved style. Lead time is 25-35 working days for a first run with dyed-to-order color, less if the fabric and shade are from stock. This batch goes live on your store.

**Step 3 — Read the data.** You run the style for a few weeks and read real sell-through, return rate, and customer feedback. Winners and losers separate themselves.

**Step 4 — Reorder winners fast (15-20 working days).** For proven styles on a stock fabric and shade, reorders skip sampling and run about 15-20 working days — the quick-response advantage. Losers are simply not reordered, and you have risked only 100 pieces, not 1,000.

**Step 5 — Scale the proven range.** As a style establishes steady demand, larger reorders bring the per-unit cost down and you lock in a standing fabric and shade band for consistency.

This loop — sample, test, read, reorder — is the operational core of modern DTC sourcing, and it depends entirely on the factory holding quality steady across every batch size.

## Part 4: Keeping quality identical from test to scale

The biggest fear brands have about small batches is that the test looks great and the scaled bulk drifts. We design against that by locking parameters at the sampling stage, not at each production run.

**Fabric and GSM.** The approved fabric quality and weight (for example 110-130 GSM for a standard modal square, heavier for winter weights) is fixed in the tech pack and used for every batch.

**Color: ΔE 1.0.** Every dye lot, in every batch size, is matched to within ΔE 1.0 of the approved lab dip. ΔE is the industry measure of color difference; 1.0 is the threshold below which the human eye struggles to see a difference. A reorder six months later should still match the original.

**Dimensional tolerance.** Finished size held to +/- 2 cm on standard squares, measured on a sampled percentage of every batch.

**Edge and stitch standards.** The named hem type (baby-rolled, pin-hem) and stitch density are specified once and repeated across runs.

**AQL 2.5 on every batch.** We inspect to AQL 2.5 (Acceptance Quality Limit, the statistical sampling standard that defines how many defects are tolerable in a batch) regardless of order size. A 100-piece test batch is inspected to the same standard as a 2,000-piece bulk run.

Because the specification lives in the tech pack and not in a single order, scaling changes the quantity and nothing else.

## Part 5: Fabric strategy for quick response

The single biggest lever on reorder speed is fabric. Dyeing and knitting are the slow steps; if they are pre-solved, reorders fly.

**Hold proven styles on stock fabric.** We keep common modal and jersey qualities in greige (undyed) stock. A proven seller on a stock quality can be dyed and finished far faster than one requiring a special knit.

**Lock a standing shade band.** For a brand's core colors, we approve a shade band once and reorder against it, so each reorder does not restart color development.

**Batch dye core colors.** Brands running a consistent palette can schedule periodic dye runs so core shades are effectively on tap.

**Reserve special fabrics for hero styles.** Custom jacquard or specialty blends justify their longer lead time only on signature pieces, not on every test. Keeping the test range on standard fabrics keeps the whole test-and-scale loop fast and cheap.

A short conversation about fabric strategy at the start of a relationship pays off every time a style goes viral and needs restocking in weeks.

## Part 6: The cost model — small batch versus bulk

Brands often ask whether small batches are 'worth it' given the higher per-unit price, and the honest answer is that the comparison should be made on total risk-adjusted cost, not sticker price per piece.

**Per-unit price.** A 100-piece run carries a higher unit cost than a 1,000-piece run because fixed costs — machine setup, the minimum dye charge, inspection labor — are spread over fewer units. There is no way around this physics, and we quote it transparently.

**Risk-adjusted cost.** The right question is not 'what does each piece cost' but 'what does each sold piece cost'. If a brand over-orders 1,000 units of a style that only sells 300, the 700 unsold units are either frozen cash or discounted to clear. The effective cost per sold piece on that bulk run can easily exceed the small-batch price. Testing at 100 pieces first, then scaling only proven winners, usually produces a lower blended cost across a whole range.

**When to scale.** Once a style shows steady sell-through, larger reorders bring the per-unit price down and the economics flip firmly in favor of volume. The test batch is not meant to be the forever order size — it is the filter that decides which styles earn a volume commitment.

Framing the decision this way helps brand owners resist the false economy of over-ordering for a lower sticker price.

## Part 7: Logistics and replenishment rhythm

Quick response is not only a production question; it is also a logistics and planning rhythm, and the two have to work together.

**Shipping mode by urgency.** A first test batch can move by economical sea freight because it is not yet time-critical. A fast reorder of a style that is selling out may justify air freight for the first restock to avoid a stockout, then revert to sea for subsequent runs. We help brands plan which mode fits each stage.

**Buffer stock on core styles.** For established hero styles, holding a modest safety stock — either at the brand's warehouse or coordinated with us — bridges the reorder lead time so the product page never goes dark.

**Consolidation.** Brands reordering several proven styles at once can consolidate them into one shipment to reduce freight cost per piece, which partly offsets the small-batch premium.

**Documentation ready.** We prepare the compliance and shipping documents (fiber content, care labeling, OEKO-TEX documentation where required) so customs clearance does not become the hidden bottleneck that erases the speed gained in production.

Planning the replenishment rhythm alongside the production plan is what turns fast manufacturing into fast shelf availability.

## Conclusion

Low-MOQ, small-batch, quick-response manufacturing is not a compromise — it is the sourcing model that fits how modest-fashion brands actually grow in 2026. Test styles small at a 100-piece MOQ, read real demand, and reorder the winners fast on standing fabric and shade, all held to the same ΔE 1.0 color, +/- 2 cm tolerance, and AQL 2.5 inspection as full bulk. The result is less cash frozen in dead stock, faster reaction to trends, and a cleaner path to scaling the styles that earn it.

QiuYan Factory supports test-and-scale programs for DTC brands, boutiques, and OEM/ODM buyers across Europe, the Gulf, and North America, producing modal, jersey, bamboo viscose, and Tencel Lyocell hijabs with a 100-pc standard MOQ, 5-7 day samples, and fast reorders on proven styles. To scope a small-batch program, email melody@wennuanfactory.com or message WhatsApp +86 150 2459 7603.

title: Hijab Fabric Opacity and Coverage: A Factory Guide to Specifying and Testing the Number One Return Driver

metaDescription: A factory-side guide to hijab fabric opacity and coverage — the top wholesale return driver. How to specify GSM, cover factor, and opacity, run the white-cloth and grey-card tests, and lock it in before AQL 2.5 bulk.
heroAlt: A draped modal hijab fabric panel on a factory inspection table showing opacity and coverage for wholesale quality control

faq.q: Why is 'fabric thinner than expected' the most common hijab complaint, and how do I prevent it?
faq.a: It happens because brands approve a style on hand-feel or a photo and never specify opacity as a measurable requirement. The fix is to lock three numbers in the tech pack before bulk: GSM (fabric weight per square meter), cover factor (how tightly the knit is constructed), and a pass/fail opacity result from a defined test. When those are approved on the sample and inspected on bulk, 'too thin' and 'see-through' stop being surprises. We help brands set realistic targets per fabric type. Email melody@wennuanfactory.com or WhatsApp +86 150 2459 7603.

faq.q: What GSM should a modal hijab be to avoid being see-through?
faq.a: For a standard everyday modal square we recommend 110-130 GSM; below roughly 100 GSM a plain modal starts to show scalp and hairline on lighter skin tones and under bright light, which is the number-one cause of returns. Winter and premium opaque lines run heavier at 140-180 GSM. But GSM alone is not enough — a loosely knit heavy fabric can still be sheer, so we pair the weight target with a cover-factor check and a direct opacity test rather than trusting weight by itself.

faq.q: How do you actually test opacity before approving bulk production?
faq.a: We use two practical checks alongside the lab data. First, the grey-card / print test: lay the single-layer fabric over a standard grey card or printed line sheet and grade how much shows through under controlled lighting. Second, we assess coverage as worn — single layer over a skin-tone board under bright light, since that is the real-world failure case.
